registers.name_in_paper: Laboratory tax-compliance experiment (LEE, University of Copenhagen, and BLESS, University of Bologna), programmed in z-Tree, with a Holt and Laury (2002) risk-elicitation task and a post-experimental questionnaire
registers.role: treatment, outcomes and controls for every regression in the paper

linkages: A participant's experimental declarations, risk-elicitation choices and post-experimental questionnaire answers are linked at the individual level through the randomly assigned client ID number used in place of names (p. 188).
Participants are linked to their session, and hence to the Pool Size variable, through the 16 experimental sessions (10 in Denmark, 6 in Italy).

sample.universe: Native undergraduate and graduate students registered in the ORSEE subject pools of the Laboratory for Experimental Economics (LEE), University of Copenhagen, and the Bologna Laboratory for Experiments in Social Science (BLESS), University of Bologna, i.e. individuals born in Denmark (Italy) to Danish (Italian) parents.
sample.unit_of_observation: Subject-round for the double-hurdle regressions (180 subjects x 9 rounds = 1,620 observations); subject for the subject-pool comparison in Table 3; EVS respondent for Table 9.
selection_rules: Recruited via ORSEE from the standing LEE and BLESS participant databases; neither the aims nor the cross-national scope of the project were stated in the invitation email or during the sessions.
Only native students, i.e. individuals born in Denmark (Italy) to Danish (Italian) parents.
16 sessions in total: 10 in Denmark (4 to 14 participants each) and 6 in Italy (18 to 25 participants each).

All participants completed the three stages (nine rounds) of the tax-compliance experiment, the Holt-Laury risk-elicitation task and the post-experimental questionnaire; the paper reports no attrition or exclusion.
sample.n_observations: 1,620 subject-round observations (Num. obs. in Tables 6 and 7)
sample.n_individuals: 180 participants: 74 Danish and 106 Italian (Num. groups = 180 in the panel DH models)

construction_notes: The study uses no Danish administrative register: all experimental variables are generated in the laboratory, and the only external data source is the European Values Study (Table 9).

Dependent variable: ER = 1 - reporting compliance rate, where the compliance rate is declared income divided by earned income; ER ranges over [0, 1] (Table 8, p. 201) and is also described as the ratio between undeclared income and total earned income (p. 190).
Income is earned in a three-minute real-effort clerical data-entry task at the start of each of the three stages; each correctly copied row pays 10 points.

Nine rounds in three stages (Table 1, p. 186): rounds 1-3 vary redistribution (none / equal / doubled then equal) at a 30% tax rate and 5% audit probability; rounds 4-6 vary the tax rate (5% / 30% / 50%); rounds 7-9 vary the audit probability (5% / 30% / 50%). The fine for detected under-reporting is twice the tax due in every round. The order of stages and rounds was deliberately not randomised.
Risk aversion is the number of safe 'Option A' choices in the ten-decision Holt and Laury (2002) lottery task (Table 2, p. 197).
Tax morale is proxied by the EVS/WVS single item on whether cheating on tax can be justified, scored 1-10; the paper treats tax morale as the complement of this tolerance measure.
Perception of others' compliance is elicited in every round immediately after the declaration decision, on a 0-5 scale.

Points were converted to local currency at a rate calibrated so that average hourly earnings matched the local student wage; mean earnings were EUR 10.641 in Italy and DKK 191.804 in Denmark, plus a show-up fee of EUR 5 in Italy and DKK 100 in Denmark.
Instructions were given in English in Denmark (a requirement of LEE) and in Italian in Bologna, translated and back-translated.

Estimation: pooled and panel double-hurdle models (Cragg, 1971) via the two-stage Engel and Moffatt (2014) procedure; the first hurdle is a probit for being an evader and the second a tobit for the level of evasion. In the panel DH models the first hurdle omits Tax Rate, Audit, Redistribution, Rows and Perception because the model has only one outcome per subject, and a subject counts as fully compliant only if she declares truthfully in all nine rounds.

claims.statement: Italian subjects are less likely than Danish subjects to be identified as tax evaders in a round (first hurdle of the pooled double-hurdle model).

treatment.label: Italy (dummy for the subject's country of origin)

Only native students were recruited, i.e. 'individuals born in Denmark (Italy) to Danish (Italian) parents' (p. 188). outcome.label: d_ij: binary indicator that subject i is identified as an evader in round j (first hurdle, extensive margin)

definition.value: First hurdle of the Cragg (1971) double-hurdle model: d_ij = 1 if the latent index d*_ij > 0 and 0 otherwise (Eqs. (2), (3) and (7), pp. 190, 192). The paper describes it as the hurdle that 'determines whether or not a person participates in evasion and is particularly suited to capture effect occurring mainly at the extensive margin' (p. 190). In the pooled DH models (1), (3), (5) and (7) the hurdle is defined round by round; in the panel DH models a subject is a non-evader only if she declares her true earnings in all nine rounds.

timing.value: Declaration decision taken in each of the nine rounds of a single ~90-minute laboratory session, academic year 2016/2017.

units.value: latent-index (probit) units of the first hurdle, per one-unit increase in the regressor

magnitude.interpretation: Table 6 also reports, in italics, the average marginal effect of this first-hurdle coefficient: -0.104.

estimand.target_population: The 180 participants of the laboratory experiment; the coefficient is a partial association in the latent-index equation of the double-hurdle model, not an experimentally identified effect.

population.description: The 180 native university students who took part in the laboratory tax-compliance experiment: 74 Danish subjects recruited at the Laboratory for Experimental Economics (LEE), University of Copenhagen (10 sessions), and 106 Italian subjects recruited at the Bologna Laboratory for Experiments in Social Science (BLESS), University of Bologna (6 sessions), each observed in nine experimental rounds (1,620 subject-round observations).
population.ages: Mainly the 20-24 age bracket; mean age 23.95 years in Denmark and 23.68 years in Italy (Table 3, p. 197)
population.selection: Self-selected volunteers from the standing ORSEE subject pools of the LEE and BLESS laboratories, restricted to native students, i.e. individuals born in Denmark (Italy) to Danish (Italian) parents; undergraduate and graduate students from various fields; neither the aims nor the cross-national scope of the project were disclosed in the invitation.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in measured individual characteristics across the 180 participants, conditioned on the other regressors of the double-hurdle model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: conditional on the other regressors of the model (the experimental parameters and the individual characteristics listed in Table 8), the regressor is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of evasion. The paper never states this assumption; it motivates the control set only by noting that risk aversion and gender proportions differ between the two samples and 'both can affect tax reporting behavior'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 (p. 197) reports a comparison of subject-pool characteristics by country; the paper offers no further defence of the conditioning set.

heterogeneity.finding: Male*Italy is positive and statistically significant in the first hurdle of pooled DH model (7) of Table 7 (0.498, SE 0.164, p < 0.01; marginal effect 0.126): being male raises evasion more in the Italian than in the Danish sample.

Risk aversion*Italy is negative and statistically significant in the second hurdle of pooled DH models (5) and (7) of Table 7 (-0.030, SE 0.012 and -0.031, SE 0.012; p < 0.05), and negative and weakly significant in the first hurdle of panel DH models (6) and (8) (-0.410, SE 0.229, p < 0.10).

Perception*Italy is positive and significant in the first hurdle of pooled DH model (3) of Table 6 (0.189, SE 0.065, p < 0.01): beliefs about others' compliance reduce evasion less for Italian than for Danish subjects.

In the panel DH models (2) and (4) of Table 6 the Italy coefficient is still negative in both hurdles but no longer statistically significant (-1.090, SE 0.832 and -0.988, SE 0.960 in the first hurdles).

value.claimed_domain: Real-world tax behaviour in Denmark and Italy beyond the student laboratory sample: the authors state that 'Denmark, it seems, is not a special case of tax compliance culture that cannot be replicated elsewhere; nor is Italy a hopeless case', that behavioural responses of students are largely the same as those of non-students in identical tax experiments, and that there is no reason to anticipate different results in other parts of Italy.

definition.value: Second hurdle (tobit) of the double-hurdle model: ER*_ij = max(ER**_ij, 0) with ER**_ij given by Eq. (8) (pp. 190, 192). The underlying dependent variable ER is the evasion rate, 'Evasion rate = 1 - reporting compliance rate, where the latter is the ratio of declared income to earned income', on [0, 1] (Table 8, p. 201); equivalently 'the ratio between undeclared income and total earned income' (p. 190). The paper describes the second hurdle as the one that 'determines the level of evasion only for those people who ever choose to evade and is therefore relevant for the effect occurring at the intensive margin' (p. 190).

definition.value: Second hurdle (tobit) of the double-hurdle model: ER*_ij = max(ER**_ij, 0) with ER**_ij given by Eq. (8) (pp. 190, 192). The underlying dependent variable ER is the evasion rate, 'Evasion rate = 1 - reporting compliance rate, where the latter is the ratio of declared income to earned income', on [0, 1] (Table 8, p. 201); equivalently 'the ratio between undeclared income and total earned income' (p. 190). The paper describes the second hurdle as the one that 'determines the level of evasion only for those people who ever choose to evade and is therefore relevant for the effect occurring at the intensive margin' (p. 190).

units.value: evasion-rate points on the [0, 1] scale of the second-hurdle tobit, per one-unit increase in the regressor

population.description: The 180 native university students who took part in the laboratory tax-compliance experiment: 74 Danish subjects recruited at the Laboratory for Experimental Economics (LEE), University of Copenhagen (10 sessions), and 106 Italian subjects recruited at the Bologna Laboratory for Experiments in Social Science (BLESS), University of Bologna (6 sessions), each observed in nine experimental rounds (1,620 subject-round observations).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in measured individual characteristics across the 180 participants, conditioned on the other regressors of the double-hurdle model.

outcome.label: d_ij: binary indicator that subject i is identified as an evader in round j (first hurdle, extensive margin)

definition.value: First hurdle of the Cragg (1971) double-hurdle model: d_ij = 1 if the latent index d*_ij > 0 and 0 otherwise (Eqs. (2), (3) and (7), pp. 190, 192). The paper describes it as the hurdle that 'determines whether or not a person participates in evasion and is particularly suited to capture effect occurring mainly at the extensive margin' (p. 190). In the pooled DH models (1), (3), (5) and (7) the hurdle is defined round by round; in the panel DH models a subject is a non-evader only if she declares her true earnings in all nine rounds.

timing.value: Declaration decision taken in each of the nine rounds of a single ~90-minute laboratory session, academic year 2016/2017.

units.value: latent-index (probit) units of the first hurdle, per one-unit increase in the regressor

magnitude.interpretation: Table 6 also reports, in italics, the average marginal effect of this first-hurdle coefficient: -0.067.

claims.statement: Having no previous participation in experimental studies does not affect the level of evasion among evaders in the pooled double-hurdle model.

treatment.label: No previous participation (in experimental studies)

definition.value: Dummy variable, '1 if no previous participation, 0 otherwise' (Table 8, p. 201), i.e. whether the subject had NOT participated previously in experimental studies. Higher values therefore mean LESS prior experimental experience.

outcome.label: ER*_ij: level of the evasion rate of subject i in round j, conditional on passing the first hurdle (second hurdle, intensive margin)

definition.value: Second hurdle (tobit) of the double-hurdle model: ER*_ij = max(ER**_ij, 0) with ER**_ij given by Eq. (8) (pp. 190, 192). The underlying dependent variable ER is the evasion rate, 'Evasion rate = 1 - reporting compliance rate, where the latter is the ratio of declared income to earned income', on [0, 1] (Table 8, p. 201); equivalently 'the ratio between undeclared income and total earned income' (p. 190). The paper describes the second hurdle as the one that 'determines the level of evasion only for those people who ever choose to evade and is therefore relevant for the effect occurring at the intensive margin' (p. 190).

timing.value: Declaration decision taken in each of the nine rounds of a single ~90-minute laboratory session, academic year 2016/2017.

units.value: evasion-rate points on the [0, 1] scale of the second-hurdle tobit, per one-unit increase in the regressor

definition.value: Discrete variable on [0, 5] measuring the subject's belief about how many other participants in the room declared their true earnings: 0 = none; 1 = less than a half; 2 = about a half; 3 = more than a half; 4 = almost everyone; 5 = everyone (Table 8, p. 201).

definition.value: Second hurdle (tobit) of the double-hurdle model: ER*_ij = max(ER**_ij, 0) with ER**_ij given by Eq. (8) (pp. 190, 192). The underlying dependent variable ER is the evasion rate, 'Evasion rate = 1 - reporting compliance rate, where the latter is the ratio of declared income to earned income', on [0, 1] (Table 8, p. 201); equivalently 'the ratio between undeclared income and total earned income' (p. 190). The paper describes the second hurdle as the one that 'determines the level of evasion only for those people who ever choose to evade and is therefore relevant for the effect occurring at the intensive margin' (p. 190).

units.value: evasion-rate points on the [0, 1] scale of the second-hurdle tobit, per one-unit increase in the regressor

claims.statement: Self-reported tolerance of tax evasion does not affect the level of evasion among evaders.

treatment.label: Tolerance of tax evasion (proxy for tax morale)

definition.value: Self-reported attitude towards tax evasion elicited in the post-experimental questionnaire with the EVS/WVS item 'Can cheating on tax if you have the chance always be justified, never be justified, or something in between?', discrete from 1 (never justified) to 10 (always justified) (Table 8, p. 201). The paper uses it as a proxy for tax morale, which it defines as the complement of tolerance for tax evasion, so a HIGHER value means LOWER tax morale.

timing.value: Elicited in the post-experimental questionnaire, after all nine rounds of the tax-compliance experiment and after the risk elicitation task.

outcome.label: ER*_ij: level of the evasion rate of subject i in round j, conditional on passing the first hurdle (second hurdle, intensive margin)

definition.value: Second hurdle (tobit) of the double-hurdle model: ER*_ij = max(ER**_ij, 0) with ER**_ij given by Eq. (8) (pp. 190, 192). The underlying dependent variable ER is the evasion rate, 'Evasion rate = 1 - reporting compliance rate, where the latter is the ratio of declared income to earned income', on [0, 1] (Table 8, p. 201); equivalently 'the ratio between undeclared income and total earned income' (p. 190). The paper describes the second hurdle as the one that 'determines the level of evasion only for those people who ever choose to evade and is therefore relevant for the effect occurring at the intensive margin' (p. 190).

units.value: evasion-rate points on the [0, 1] scale of the second-hurdle tobit, per one-unit increase in the regressor

population.selection: Self-selected volunteers from the standing ORSEE subject pools of the LEE and BLESS laboratories, restricted to native students, i.e. individuals born in Denmark (Italy) to Danish (Italian) parents; undergraduate and graduate students from various fields; neither the aims nor the cross-national scope of the project were disclosed in the invitation.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in measured individual characteristics across the 180 participants, conditioned on the other regressors of the double-hurdle model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: conditional on the other regressors of the model (the experimental parameters and the individual characteristics listed in Table 8), the regressor is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of evasion. The paper never states this assumption; it motivates the control set only by noting that risk aversion and gender proportions differ between the two samples and 'both can affect tax reporting behavior'.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 (p. 197) reports a comparison of subject-pool characteristics by country; the paper offers no further defence of the conditioning set.

links.pointer_quote: Our results show that Danes are more likely to evade tax than Italians, and that individuals' attitudes toward tax do not significantly predict their actual evasion choices.

anchor_quote.text: All the regression models controlled for individual performance in the clerical task and subject pool size (see the variables Rows and Pool Size), but we found these variables had no impact on tax behavior.

definition.value: Interaction between the discrete Tolerance of Tax Evasion score (1-10) and the Italy dummy; it equals the tolerance score for Italian subjects and 0 for Danish subjects. Entered in the interaction vector z_i of models (3), (4) in Table 6 and (5)-(8) in Table 7.

definition.value: First hurdle of the Cragg (1971) double-hurdle model: d_ij = 1 if the latent index d*_ij > 0 and 0 otherwise (Eqs. (2), (3) and (7), pp. 190, 192). The paper describes it as the hurdle that 'determines whether or not a person participates in evasion and is particularly suited to capture effect occurring mainly at the extensive margin' (p. 190). In the pooled DH models (1), (3), (5) and (7) the hurdle is defined round by round; in the panel DH models a subject is a non-evader only if she declares her true earnings in all nine rounds.

timing.value: Declaration decision taken in each of the nine rounds of a single ~90-minute laboratory session, academic year 2016/2017.

units.value: latent-index (probit) units of the first hurdle, per one-unit increase in the regressor

definition.value: Second hurdle (tobit) of the double-hurdle model: ER*_ij = max(ER**_ij, 0) with ER**_ij given by Eq. (8) (pp. 190, 192). The underlying dependent variable ER is the evasion rate, 'Evasion rate = 1 - reporting compliance rate, where the latter is the ratio of declared income to earned income', on [0, 1] (Table 8, p. 201); equivalently 'the ratio between undeclared income and total earned income' (p. 190). The paper describes the second hurdle as the one that 'determines the level of evasion only for those people who ever choose to evade and is therefore relevant for the effect occurring at the intensive margin' (p. 190).

definition.value: First hurdle of the Cragg (1971) double-hurdle model: d_ij = 1 if the latent index d*_ij > 0 and 0 otherwise (Eqs. (2), (3) and (7), pp. 190, 192). The paper describes it as the hurdle that 'determines whether or not a person participates in evasion and is particularly suited to capture effect occurring mainly at the extensive margin' (p. 190). In the pooled DH models (1), (3), (5) and (7) the hurdle is defined round by round; in the panel DH models a subject is a non-evader only if she declares her true earnings in all nine rounds.

population.description: The 180 native university students who took part in the laboratory tax-compliance experiment: 74 Danish subjects recruited at the Laboratory for Experimental Economics (LEE), University of Copenhagen (10 sessions), and 106 Italian subjects recruited at the Bologna Laboratory for Experiments in Social Science (BLESS), University of Bologna (6 sessions), each observed in nine experimental rounds (1,620 subject-round observations).

units.value: percentage points (Denmark minus Italy) of the share of the subject pool giving this answer
